blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Labeled Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (S1GRD) datasets remain scarce, limiting supervised deep learning for land-surface remote sensing, while self-supervised pretraining for this domain has been dominated by Vision Transformer (ViT)-based masked image modeling requiring substantial data and compute. We propose SparK-SAR, a sparse convolutional masked pretraining framework built on SparK and ConvNeXt, designed to exploit convolutional inductive biases for S1GRD imagery under constrained compute. SparK-SAR makes three core technical contributions: (i) ConvNeXt-RS, a domain-adapted encoder that halves the stem stride (4x to 2x) to produce 14x14 feature maps at stride 16x, providing 4x more spatial tokens at identical parameter count; (ii) a lightweight ConvNeXt-512 reconstruction decoder with PixelShuffle upsampling that reduces pretraining VRAM by 7.5-8.5% per GPU relative to a UNet-128 baseline while matching its accuracy; and (iii) an empirical characterization of FP16 mixed-precision pretraining instability in the standard SparK UNet-768 decoder on S1GRD data, complemented by a finding that finetuning with layer-wise learning rate decay (LLRD) improves downstream performance of pretrained encoders. On four Copernicus-Bench S1GRD tasks, our finetuned 27.8M-parameter ConvNeXt-RS encoder improves over a non-pretrained baseline by +4.7, +5.0, +5.8, and +1.4 pp on EuroSAT-S1, BigEarthNet-S1, DFC2020-S1, and Flood-S1 respectively, and outperforms the Copernicus-FM ViT (139M parameters, frozen) on three of four tasks at roughly 5x fewer parameters. A pretraining data-scaling study reveals task-dependent data efficiency: classification saturates with as little as 10-25% of the SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 corpus, while dense prediction continues to improve significantly up to 25-50%. The study also includes a CKA representation analysis and a geographic de-collision experiment.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Unlike optical sensors, synthetic aperture radar (SAR)
satellites image the land surface using
microwave backscatter rather than reflected sunlight, enabling
all-weather, day-and-night acquisition well suited to land-cover
mapping, flood assessment, and environmental change monitoring,
particularly in regions where persistent cloud cover limits optical
observation ( Moreira et al., 2013 ) . Since its 2014 launch, ESA’s
Sentinel-1 mission has revisited most of the globe every 6–12 days,
accumulating a large and continually growing archive of freely
available Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (S1GRD)
imagery ( European Space Agency, 2012 ) . This unlabeled archive is abundant,
but SAR imagery is difficult for non-experts to interpret visually,
making manual annotation of large SAR scenes highly labor intensive.
Publicly available labeled SAR benchmarks have therefore stayed small
relative to computer vision norms, which in turn limits how well
supervised deep learning models can perform on SAR downstream
tasks ( Wang et al., 2022 ) .

blocks.en:
Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers one route to transferable
representations without relying on manually labeled data, and masked image
modeling (MIM) ( He et al., 2022 ; Xie et al., 2022 ) is a natural fit for
S1GRD pretraining specifically: it requires no S1GRD-appropriate
photometric augmentation scheme of the kind contrastive methods
depend on ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , and it naturally yields the dense,
patch-level representations that earth observation’s dense prediction
tasks need. Existing MIM implementations, however, are almost all
built on Vision Transformer (ViT) ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) encoders,
which typically demand large pretraining corpora and heavy compute to
perform well; Copernicus-FM ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , for instance,
needed 512 GPU hours on 4 × \times A100 GPUs and multi-modal inputs spanning
four Sentinel missions (Sentinel-1, 2, 3, 5P) to reach competitive results.

blocks.en:
For many research groups and applied teams working with SAR data,
matching the compute scale needed to pretrain these large foundation
models is itself out of reach. We therefore restrict this study’s
primary comparisons to end-to-end finetuned convolutional neural
network (CNN) encoders rather than reporting frozen ViT foundation
model backbones as directly finetuned baselines. This is not solely a
matter of compute: Copernicus-Bench’s own published learning-rate
search for these models ( 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 10 − 3 10^{-3} , 10 − 2 10^{-2} ) was
validated only for frozen-backbone and decoder-head finetuning, not
for full end-to-end finetuning, so no full-finetuning result for
these architectures could be defended as using a properly validated
learning rate. Reporting one without a fair hyperparameter search
would conflate architectural differences with an unvalidated
finetuning setup rather than isolate them. A rigorous evaluation of
full fine-tuning for these foundation models, encompassing an
architecture-specific learning-rate search, appropriate regularization
schedules, and comparable per-model tuning budgets, would constitute a
dedicated study in its own right and lies outside this paper’s scope.
The frozen-encoder results we do report (Table 6 ) are
included only as a reference point, not as the primary comparison.

blocks.en:
Building on these two lines of work, we introduce SparK-SAR: a
high-resolution sparse masked pretraining framework for S1GRD imagery
that combines SparK ( Tian et al., 2023 ) and
ConvNeXt ( Liu et al., 2022 ) and is designed to run under a
constrained compute budget. We structure our contributions around
three questions: whether sparse convolutional masked pretraining,
previously developed and validated only on natural images, can be
adapted to produce transferable representations for S1GRD SAR imagery
under constrained compute; how much pretraining data and downstream
labeled data this benefit actually requires; and whether the observed
gains are genuine, rather than an artifact of geographic overlap
between the pretraining corpus and the downstream evaluation sets.

blocks.en:
Adapting sparse masked pretraining to S1GRD SAR imagery. 1. ConvNeXt-RS encoder : a domain-adapted ConvNeXt
encoder for SAR dense prediction, reducing stem stride from 4 × 4{\times} to 2 × 2{\times} to produce 14 × 14 14{\times}14 feature
maps (stride 16 × 16{\times} ) instead of the standard 7 × 7 7{\times}7 (stride 32 × 32{\times} ), providing 4 × 4{\times} more spatial tokens
at identical parameter count (Section 3.1 ). 2. Lightweight reconstruction decoders : documentation of
FP16 mixed precision pretraining instability with the standard UNet-768
decoder on S1GRD data, and evaluation of UNet-128 and ConvNeXt-512 alternatives
that stabilize pretraining, with ConvNeXt-512 reducing pretraining VRAM
by 7.5–8.5% per GPU at matched accuracy (Section 3.2 ). 3. LLRD finetuning recipe : a finding that layer-wise
learning rate decay (LLRD) improves downstream task performance and
reduces across-seed variance when finetuning the UNet-128-pretrained
SparK encoder, but does not help a non-pretrained one (Section 3.4 ). Evaluated across four Copernicus-Bench S1GRD tasks ( Wang et al., 2025b ) spanning classification, multi-label classification, semantic
segmentation, and change detection, the resulting 27.8M-parameter
encoder improves over a non-pretrained baseline by + 4.7 +4.7 pp, + 5.0 +5.0 pp, + 5.8 +5.8 pp, and + 1.4 +1.4 pp on EuroSAT-S1, BigEarthNet-S1,
DFC2020-S1, and Flood-S1 respectively (Section 4.3 ).
Despite using a 27.8M-parameter encoder, roughly 5 × 5{\times} smaller than Copernicus-FM ViT’s 139M (frozen) parameters, our
finetuned model beats it on three of the four tasks, and it likewise
beats SoftCon ( Wang et al., 2024 ) on three of four tasks and both
CROMA ( Fuller et al., 2023 ) and DOFA ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) on all
four. The comparatively modest Flood-S1 gain is examined further in a
dedicated ceiling ablation (Section 4.4.4 ), which
points to a boundary condition for this approach: single-image masked
pretraining appears to transfer less effectively to temporal change
detection than to single-scene interpretation tasks.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work

blocks.en: 2.1 Masked Image Modeling
blocks.zh: 2.1 蒙面图像建模

blocks.en:
Building on masked language modeling ( Devlin et al., 2019 ) , masked
image modeling (MIM) has become the leading approach to
self-supervised visual pretraining. MAE ( He et al., 2022 ) showed that
reconstructing raw pixels from a small visible subset (as little as
25%) of ViT patches produces representations that transfer well at
scale, and SimMIM ( Xie et al., 2022 ) carried the same
reconstruction objective over to hierarchical Swin
Transformers ( Liu et al., 2021 ) . I-JEPA ( Assran et al., 2023 ) took a different route, predicting
latent representations of the masked regions instead of pixel values,
which pushes the model toward semantic structure over low-level
texture.

blocks.en:
These ViT-based approaches are effective but data- and
compute-hungry. Convolutional alternatives have narrowed that gap:
MCMAE ( Gao et al., 2022 ) combines convolution and transformer blocks
in a hybrid masked autoencoder, while SparK ( Tian et al., 2023 ) , the
framework this work builds on, shows that sparse masked modeling
works directly on purely hierarchical CNNs
(ResNet ( He et al., 2016 ) , ConvNeXt ( Liu et al., 2022 ) ) with no
transformer component at all. MMEarth ( Nedungadi et al., 2024 ) is
a concurrent example in the electro-optical remote sensing domain, pairing a
ConvNeXt V2 ( Woo et al., 2023 ) backbone with multi-modal MIM
objectives on electro-optical Sentinel-2 imagery; we pursue the same
CNN MIM direction on a different modality, applying it to
SAR-only pretraining under the SparK framework.

blocks.en: 2.2 Self-Supervised Learning for Remote Sensing
blocks.zh: 2.2 自行监督的遥感学习

blocks.en:
In their survey of SSL for remote sensing, Wang et al. (2022) group existing methods into two dominant
paradigms, contrastive and generative.
blocks.zh:
Wang等人在对SSL进行遥感测量时表示, (2022) 将现有方法分为两种
模式、对比性和遗传性。

blocks.en:
Among the contrastive methods,
SeCo ( Mañas et al., 2021 ) builds positive pairs from seasonal
multi-temporal imagery, and GASSL ( Ayush et al., 2021 ) instead treats
geographic co-location as a proxy for scene similarity. Both,
however, rely on augmentation pipelines built around electro-optical
statistics, which do not transfer cleanly to SAR backscatter.

blocks.en:
MIM has also been adopted for electro-optical remote sensing.
SatMAE ( Cong et al., 2022 ) adapted MAE for multi-spectral and
multi-temporal satellite data. Scale-MAE ( Reed et al., 2023 ) introduced scale-aware positional encodings for images at varying
ground sample distances. FG-MAE ( Wang et al., 2025a ) proposed
feature-guided reconstruction targets better aligned with semantic
downstream tasks.

blocks.en:
A separate line of work pairs Sentinel-1 SAR with electro-optical
data rather than treating SAR in isolation. SoftCon ( Wang et al., 2024 ) pretrains contrastively across multispectral and SAR imagery using
multi-label land-cover supervision as guidance. DOFA ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) takes a different route, using a dynamic spectral adapter, so that a single
ViT can ingest whatever sensor modality it is given.
CROMA ( Fuller et al., 2023 ) instead unifies contrastive and
masked autoencoding objectives within one radar-optical model, and
Copernicus-FM ( Wang et al., 2025b ) pushes this further still,
training a multi-modal ViT across four Sentinel missions on 18.7M
aligned images at a reported cost of roughly 512 GPU hours on NVIDIA
A100 GPUs. These models perform well, but their multi-modal inputs
and near-exclusive reliance on frozen-encoder evaluation make them a
poor match for the SAR-only, constrained-compute setting this work
targets.

blocks.en: 2.3 SAR-Specific Self-Supervised Learning
blocks.zh: 2.3 SAR-特定自我监督学习

blocks.en:
Compared to optical imagery, SSL research targeting SAR data
exclusively is still comparatively unexplored. Allen et al. (2023) demonstrated that large-scale MAE
pretraining on Sentinel-1 S1GRD data can substantially reduce label
requirements across two downstream tasks, vegetation-cover prediction
and land-cover classification, with the pretraining benefit
generalizing geographically and increasing, rather than merely
holding up, on regions outside the pretraining set.

与光学图像相比,SSL针对合成孔径雷达数据的研究
完全没有加以探讨。 艾伦等人. (2023年)证明,大规模MAE
S1GRD数据预训可大幅降低标签
植被覆盖预测

将地域和增长普遍化,而不仅仅是
坚持住,在预训范围以外的地区。

blocks.en:
SAR-JEPA ( Li et al., 2024 ) introduced a joint-embedding
predictive architecture (JEPA)-based approach for
SAR automatic target recognition (ATR) by predicting multi-scale
gradient features rather than raw pixels. SARATR-X ( Li et al., 2025 ) subsequently incorporated multi-scale gradient features into a masked
image modeling framework, using a two-step self-supervised procedure
that first performed MIM pretraining on ImageNet to obtain a
favorable weight initialization, then continued MIM pretraining on a
curated corpus of unlabeled SAR target samples using the multi-scale
gradient features to suppress speckle noise, rather than the
joint-embedding predictive approach SAR-JEPA uses. However, both
models are trained and evaluated exclusively on ATR tasks, limiting
the generalizability to land-cover and change detection problems.

Applying DINO ( Caron et al., 2021 ) -style self-distillation to SAR

decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} ), OneCycleLR with final_div_factor = 100 =100 , 50
epochs (4 warmup), FP32, under a separate codebase running PyTorch
2.1.2 and CUDA 11.8. Pretraining and finetuning therefore run on different framework
versions; we did not isolate the effect of this difference.

blocks.en:
Task-specific finetuning follows the Copernicus-Bench protocol: EuroSAT-S1
uses a linear classification head, while BigEarthNet-S1’s multi-label
classification task is trained with a multi-label soft-margin loss.
The two dense prediction tasks, DFC2020-S1 and Flood-S1,
both employ a UPerNet ( Xiao et al., 2018 ) decoder augmented with an auxiliary FCN head. For DFC2020-S1 this decoder
operates directly on the multi-scale features produced by the ConvNeXt-RS
encoder; for Flood-S1, it instead operates on the difference between
multi-scale features computed separately for the pre- and post-event
images. The ConvNeXt-RS backbone is finetuned end-to-end throughout
instead of being kept frozen.

blocks.en:
Inputs are resized to the resolution specified by the Copernicus-Bench
benchmark protocol for each task. EuroSAT-S1 (native 64 × 64 64{\times}64 ) and
BigEarthNet-S1 (native 120 × 120 120{\times}120 ) are upsampled to 224 × 224 224{\times}224 using bilinear interpolation. Flood-S1 is already native at 224 × 224 224{\times}224 , so no resizing is applied.
DFC2020-S1 is kept at its native 256 × 256 256{\times}256 resolution rather than
being unified to 224 × 224 224{\times}224 like the other three tasks.
We retain each task’s benchmark-specified resolution,
rather than unifying all four to a single value,
to keep our evaluation as directly comparable to the published
Copernicus-Bench baselines as our full-finetuning setting allows
(Section 1 ). For DFC2020-S1 and Flood-S1, resizing (where
applied) is performed jointly on the image and the segmentation mask,
using paired image-mask transformations, with bilinear interpolation for
the image and nearest-neighbor interpolation for the mask so that resizing
does not blend adjacent class labels into fractional, non-existent
intermediate values at boundaries. Because ConvNeXt-RS is a fully
convolutional encoder with no fixed-input-size constraint from positional
embeddings, it accepts both resolutions directly, with the stride-16
feature map scaling accordingly ( 14 × 14 14{\times}14 for 224 × 224 224{\times}224 inputs vs. 16 × 16 16{\times}16 for DFC2020-S1’s 256 × 256 256{\times}256 ).

blocks.en:
Despite having roughly 5 × 5{\times} fewer parameters than
Copernicus-FM ViT (27.8M vs. 139M, frozen encoder), our finetuned
model still comes out ahead on three of the four tasks: EuroSAT-S1
( 88.49 ± 0.16 88.49{\scriptstyle\pm 0.16} vs. 87.2 ± 0.1 87.2{\pm}0.1 %), DFC2020-S1
( 56.00 ± 0.08 56.00{\scriptstyle\pm 0.08} vs. 52.4 ± 0.1 52.4{\pm}0.1 %), and Flood-S1
( 80.21 ± 0.10 80.21{\scriptstyle\pm 0.10} vs. 77.7 ± 0.0 77.7{\pm}0.0 %).

On BigEarthNet-S1, SparK-SAR ( 77.03 ± 0.40 77.03{\scriptstyle\pm 0.40} ) falls marginally
below Copernicus-FM ( 77.9 ± 0.0 77.9{\pm}0.0 %) and SoftCon ( 78.7 ± 0.0 78.7{\pm}0.0 %)
under frozen evaluation.
We note that Copernicus-FM incorporates tile geographic coordinates
as an additional input modality via hypernetwork
encodings ( Wang et al., 2025b ) .
BigEarthNet-S1 labels are derived from the CORINE Land Cover
map ( Sumbul et al., 2019 ; European Environment Agency, 2020 ) , which exhibits strong
geographic clustering of land-cover classes across Europe.
It is therefore possible that Copernicus-FM’s frozen score on this
task partly reflects a geographic coordinate prior rather than purely
learned SAR representations.
SoftCon’s strong result likely reflects its multi-label land-cover
guidance during pretraining ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , which directly
benefits this multi-label classification task.

blocks.en:

entire decoder-capacity range.

blocks.en:
To complement the downstream performance analysis, we compute
Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) between
encoder representations at different pretraining data fractions.
CKA measures linear representational similarity between two neural
networks on a shared set of inputs.

We extract Stage 3 post global average pooling features ( [ N , 384 ] [N,384] )
from all eight pretrained encoders (0–100%) on each Copernicus-Bench
S1GRD test set, and compute pairwise unbiased linear CKA with Z-score
feature standardization ( Nguyen et al., 2021 ) to mitigate channel
variance skew.

blocks.en:
We use Stage 3 rather than the final Stage 4 representation because GAP
over the 14 × 14 14{\times}14 Stage 4 output would collapse the spatial
structure that our resolution ablation specifically shows to be valuable,
whereas Stage 4 features retained at full resolution ( [ N , 14 , 14 , 768 ] [N,14,14,768] )

still providing a compact, fixed-size representation for similarity
comparison. This choice is also consistent with recent evidence that
task-relevant information is often more accessible in intermediate
layers than in final-layer embeddings across several self-supervised
remote sensing architectures ( Romero et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en: 4.8 Geographic Data Overlap Analysis
blocks.zh: 4.8 地理数据重叠分析

blocks.en:
SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 and the Copernicus-Bench evaluation sets both draw
from the Sentinel-1 archive and share similar global geographic
sampling strategies, raising the possibility of geographic overlap
between pretraining and evaluation data.
To assess whether our reported gains are inflated by such overlap,
we identify pretraining tiles with geographic proximity to test set
samples using task-specific thresholds derived from the physical patch
dimensions of each dataset pair, given a Sentinel-1 GSD of
10 m/pixel: 1,640 m for EuroSAT-S1, 1,920 m for BigEarthNet-S1,
and 2,440 m for Flood-S1. DFC2020-S1 is not assessed due to the
absence of coordinate metadata in the dataset release.
Under these thresholds, 10.9% of EuroSAT-S1 test samples, 4.3% of
BigEarthNet-S1 test samples, and 10.1% of Flood-S1 test samples have
at least one geographically proximate pretraining tile; from the
pretraining side, only 1,406 of 243,968 SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 tiles (0.58%)
are implicated across all three assessable tasks combined.

blocks.en:
To directly test whether this overlap inflates our reported gains, we
re-pretrain SparK-SAR from scratch on a de-collided version of
SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 with all 1,406 overlapping tiles removed (242,562
remaining), and re-finetune on all four downstream tasks (5 seeds
each). The de-collided model was pretrained (FP16 mixed precision, global batch
size 256) on a single NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPU
and finetuned (FP32) on single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs, whereas the original models were
pretrained on 4 × \times V100 32 GB GPUs (64 samples per GPU) and finetuned on V100 GPUs;
the remainder of the recipe is unchanged, so hardware and per-device batch size are
minor additional differences between the two columns of Table 13 .
Table 13 reports the results: all four tasks
change by less than 0.1 percentage points relative to the original
pretraining, within one standard deviation, confirming that the
reported gains are not attributable to geographic leakage. DFC2020-S1
remains an open limitation for the overlap analysis itself, since its
dataset release provides no coordinate metadata to check test-set
proximity directly; its unchanged performance under the de-collided
checkpoint above offers indirect reassurance only.

Of the three design changes evaluated, the higher-resolution
ConvNeXt-RS encoder matters most for dense prediction: its gains are
largest on segmentation and change detection, which is exactly the
signal we would expect if the standard stride- 32 × 32{\times} ConvNeXt is
simply too coarse for SAR pixel-level tasks. Halving the stem stride
fixes this without adding a single parameter.

The decoder ablation (Section 4.4.2 ) tells a

indistinguishable downstream accuracy ( p = 0.17 p{=}0.17 ), so whatever the
original SparK recipe’s hierarchical decoder buys on natural images,
it is not required to transfer well to S1GRD at a matched learning
rate. That makes ConvNeXt-512 the better default whenever VRAM is
tight, since it recovers 7.5–8.5% per GPU (hardware-dependent) for
no accuracy cost. LLRD, meanwhile, is a smaller but broadly positive
lever for the UNet-128-pretrained encoder: mean performance improves and
variance shrinks across all four tasks, reaching significance on two of them
after correction (Section 4.4.3 ), enough that we recommend
it as a default for pretrained encoders rather than an optional extra; it did
not help a non-pretrained encoder (Section 3.4 ).

blocks.en:
The data scaling analysis reveals that SAR MIM pretraining is
remarkably data-efficient: classification tasks and change detection
saturate with as few as 10–25% of the pretraining corpus (24,396
tiles), while dense semantic segmentation (DFC2020-S1) keeps improving
significantly up to 25% (60,992 tiles) and continues to gain, more
gradually, through 50% (121,984 tiles).
This saturation behavior suggests that the limited visual diversity
of SAR amplitude imagery, which is typically dominated by a relatively
small number of backscatter regimes corresponding to major land-cover
types, can be effectively characterized by a surprisingly small
pretraining corpus.
Consequently, researchers need not curate massive SAR datasets to
benefit from the SparK-SAR pretraining method; a geographically diverse
collection of ∼ \sim 25,000 tiles may be sufficient for most
applications.

The broader case our results build is a practical one: for SAR
remote sensing, a compute-efficient, domain-specific CNN

modality, on four V100 32 GB GPUs, in under a day, holds its own

parameters and orders of magnitude more pretraining data and compute

blocks.en: 6 Conclusions
blocks.zh: 6. 结论

blocks.en:
This work investigates how masked self-supervised pretraining can be
adapted to the particular characteristics of Sentinel-1 GRD imagery.
The proposed SparK-SAR framework combines a high-resolution ConvNeXt-RS
encoder producing 14 × 14 14{\times}14 feature maps with lightweight
reconstruction decoders designed to avoid the numerical difficulties
observed during mixed-precision pretraining on SAR data.
Together with layer-wise learning rate decay during finetuning,
these modifications enable a 27.8M-parameter encoder to transfer
effectively to four distinct Copernicus-Bench S1GRD downstream tasks
within a limited computational budget.

The experiments also provide evidence that increasing pretraining data
does not yield uniform benefits across downstream tasks.
The 27.8M-parameter encoder exceeds the performance of frozen
ViT-based encoders with as much as 5 × 5{\times} more parameters on
three of the four evaluated tasks.
Moreover, the data-scaling experiments show that classification
performance largely reaches saturation after using 10–25% of the
SSL4EO-S12 v1.1 corpus, whereas dense prediction tasks continue to
improve significantly up to 25% and keep gaining, more gradually,
through 50% of the training set.
CKA analysis provides a complementary view of this behavior:
as more data is introduced, the learned representations progressively
approach those obtained with the full pretraining set, following trends
that are consistent with the observed downstream results.

blocks.en:
Taken together, the findings indicate that effective SAR representation
learning can be achieved without relying exclusively on very large-scale
pretraining. Compact CNN models, when paired with objectives and
architectures adapted to SAR characteristics, can provide useful
representations with substantially lower computational requirements.
At the same time, the task-dependent scaling behavior highlights limitations
of single-image pretraining, particularly for temporal change analysis.
Future work will therefore investigate pretraining objectives that explicitly
exploit multi-temporal observations, as well as extensions to interferometric
SAR that incorporate phase and coherence alongside amplitude information.
